outcome: Jineon Baek posted a 119-page arXiv preprint (Nov 29, 2024) claiming a proof that Gerver's 1992 sofa (area ≈2.2195) is the global optimum, resolving the problem as stated; the claim has been widely reported since Dec 2024 but as of the most recent sources found (mid-2026) is still under peer review at Annals of Mathematics and has not been formally accepted or digested by an expert review/verification, so it is coded as a claim rather than a resolution.

ai.basis_quote: We report two approaches, both supporting Gerver's conjecture that his shape is the unique global maximum... It turns out that the upper bound yielded by our models does converge to Gerver's area (within an error of 0.01% when the number of angles reaches 2100). We also improve their five-angle upper bound from 2.37 to 2.3337.

summary: Two distinct events occurred in the window, and they have different relationships to the problem and to AI. (1) In July 2024, Leng, Bi, Cha, Pinilla and Thiyagalingam (arXiv:2407.11106) used neural networks — a piecewise-linear network trained via physics-informed machine learning to model corridor rotation/trajectory, plus a discrete-optimization approach to the Kallus-Romik upper bound scaled to 10,000 angles — to produce numerical evidence that Gerver's sofa is optimal, and concretely tightened the best known five-angle upper bound from 2.37 to 2.3337. This is genuine AI involvement that moved a published bound, but the problem remained open afterward, so under the rules this is `progress`/`bound`, not a resolution, and does not by itself change `status`. (2) In November 2024, Jineon Baek (Yonsei University) posted a 119-page arXiv preprint, 'Optimality of Gerver's Sofa,' giving a purely human, non-computer-assisted proof (representing sofas as points in an infinite-dimensional space and using a function Q) that Gerver's construction with 18 curve sections attains the maximum area exactly, which if correct fully resolves the problem as Wikipedia states it. This was widely reported (Quanta Feb 2025, Scientific American Dec 2024 and its 2025 'Top 10 Math Discoveries' list, NPR Dec 2024, Korea Herald, etc.) but every source consulted, including the most recent (a Jan 2026 Seoul Economic Daily piece and general 2026 searches), describes the proof as still under peer review at the Annals of Mathematics, with no announcement of acceptance, no published expert digestion working through the argument, and no errata or revised arXiv version (still v1) found. Because no human expert's review of the full argument was found to be complete and public, the decisive event is coded `claimed` rather than `resolved`, dated to the November 29, 2024 preprint submission (the first public written argument), with `resolution_direction` confirmed (the result proves the conjectured answer). The AI-involved paper is a separate, non-decisive event, recorded here as an example of AI moving a bound (`ai_role: bound`) but not driving the record's status, since the status rests on Baek's proof, which used no AI.
competing_reading: If Annals of Mathematics has in fact accepted the paper or a leading expert (e.g., a colloquium talk write-up, a detailed referee report made public, or a blog post working through the proof) has publicly and specifically vetted the full argument sometime after the searches reported here (last done via sources dated through mid-2026), the correct status would be `resolved` rather than `claimed`, still dated to the November 2024 preprint under the dating rule (§6.3: date the first public written argument, not the journal publication). I found no such digestion, but journal review timelines for a 119-page proof in a top journal can span years without much public signal in between, so I cannot rule out an acceptance that simply wasn't covered by press in the sources I could reach.
what_would_settle_it: An Annals of Mathematics acceptance notice or publication, a detailed public referee/expert write-up (e.g. a Tao-style blog post or a survey working through Baek's argument), or a revised arXiv version addressing referee comments, any of which would move the status from `claimed` to `resolved` (still dated to the original Nov 2024 preprint).
